title: The Mushroom Map
dek: Seattle told the cops to leave psychedelics alone. The state didn't. What's legal right now, what's coming in 2027, and why it's not as simple as your roommate thinks.
body: Seattle told the cops to leave the mushrooms alone back in 2021. That does not mean mushrooms are legal. Five years later, the gap between what this city tolerates, what Washington allows and what the federal government will actually sign off on is wide enough to drive a Volkswagen bus through. Here's the map.
## What's legal right now, nationally
= Psilocybin, MDMA, LSD, DMT, ibogaine | Schedule I: illegal
= Ketamine for depression | Legal, off-label
= Spravato (esketamine nasal spray) | FDA-approved
= FDA-approved classic psychedelic | None yet

Under federal law, psilocybin, MDMA, LSD, DMT, mescaline and ibogaine are still Schedule I: officially no accepted medical use, and illegal outside licensed research. No classic psychedelic has FDA approval as of this issue.

Ketamine is the loophole everybody already walks through. It's Schedule III and only FDA-approved as an anesthetic, so every depression clinic using it is doing so off-label, which is legal with a prescriber. The FDA has warned about compounded at-home ketamine, and federal prosecutors and the DEA have gone after some tele-ketamine prescribers. Spravato, the esketamine nasal spray, is FDA-approved for depression that hasn't responded to at least two antidepressants, and since January 2025 it can be used on its own. It comes with strings: certified clinics, at least two hours of monitoring, and a ride home.
## What's legal in Washington

Short version: nothing new under state law. Possession of psilocybin is a gross misdemeanor under the 2023 'Blake fix': up to six months and $1,000 for the first two offenses and up to 364 days after that, with diversion and treatment encouraged.
What we have instead is a growing list of places where police are told to look the other way:
= Seattle, 2021 | Lowest enforcement priority
= Port Townsend, 2021 | Lowest enforcement priority
= Olympia, 2024 | Lowest enforcement priority
= Tacoma, 2025 | Lowest enforcement priority
= Unincorporated King County, March 2026 | Lowest enforcement priority

Seattle's resolution covers growing and non-commercial sharing for spiritual, healing or personal-growth practices. Selling is still out. And these are enforcement priorities, not law. State police and prosecutors can still act.
> This is not a decriminalization motion. It is a deprioritization effort here in King County (Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda)
Not everyone is on board. Councilmember Reagan Dunn, who voted no, warned these are not harmless drugs.

Olympia keeps flirting with a real program. A 2023 law, SB 5263, set up a psilocybin task force and a UW pilot for veterans and first responders, but then-Gov. Inslee vetoed the advisory board. UW's study of psilocybin for veterans and first responders with alcohol use disorder and PTSD closed enrollment in June. This year's attempt at a medical psilocybin program, SB 5921, cleared a Senate committee in February and then died in Ways & Means. The earliest anyone could try again is the 2027 session.
## What's legal down the road

Oregon voted in licensed psilocybin services in 2020. More than 10,000 people have been through it, but about a third of the licensed service centers have closed. A high-end session runs about $3,000, and roughly 60 percent of clients come from out of state. Colorado has 34 licensed healing centers charging around $3,500 for a full course. New Mexico's Medical Psilocybin Act aims to treat its first patients by the end of 2026. Texas set aside $50 million for ibogaine research, but nobody met the required private match, so the money is stuck.
No statewide psychedelics measure made the November 3 ballot. Alaska's campaign came up short and is aiming for 2028.
## What's on the horizon

This is where it gets wild. In April, President Trump signed an executive order to speed up psychedelic treatments for serious mental illness, including fast-track vouchers and quick DEA rescheduling of anything the FDA approves. A week later the FDA handed priority vouchers, worth a review of a month or two, to Compass Pathways and the nonprofit Usona Institute for psilocybin, and to Transcend Therapeutics for a PTSD drug called methylone.
= Compass psilocybin, treatment-resistant depression | Filing by end of 2026
= Possible first approval and launch | Early 2027
= MDMA for PTSD (refiled, no new trial) | No date
= LSD for anxiety (Definium, formerly MindMed) | Phase 3 positive
= Washington medical psilocybin | 2027 session at earliest

Compass says its two big trials, more than 1,000 people, hit their targets, and it expects to finish its FDA filing by the end of this year and possibly launch early in 2027. Even then, the drug would need to be moved off Schedule I. The MDMA company that got rejected in 2024 has quietly refiled without the new trial the FDA asked for. And the LSD company now called Definium reported positive late-stage results for generalized anxiety.
## The bad trip

Not everyone is cheering. The FDA's 2024 rejection of MDMA therapy cited problems including patients figuring out whether they got the drug, allegations that some researchers coached patients, and concerns about heart problems and abuse. Three MDMA therapy papers were retracted that year.
> We are literally seeing politics put over science. (Rep. Jake Auchincloss, on the White House voucher push)

A Penn medical ethicist called the political fast-tracking completely absurd and really terrifying. The FDA says the drugs' development must be grounded in sound science. Ibogaine carries a risk of life-threatening heart rhythm problems. And price is the quiet killer: legal psilocybin runs thousands of dollars a session and insurance doesn't cover state programs.
## The Report's take

Seattle has been ahead of the law for five years, and the law is finally jogging to catch up. If Compass gets approved, you could see prescription psilocybin in early 2027, in a clinic, with a price tag, under supervision. Until then, the cops may not care, but the state still does. Know the difference before you find out the hard way.
If you're struggling with depression or PTSD right now, talk to a doctor about what's legal today. Ketamine clinics and Spravato are real, prescription options in this city.
